nameStory: Common sorrel gets its name from the Old French word 'surelle,' meaning 'sour,' which perfectly describes the tangy, lemony taste of its leaves. The word 'sorrel' is related to 'sour' - just take a nibble and you'll understand why! It's also called 'garden sorrel' because it's been cultivated for centuries as a culinary herb.
description: Common sorrel is a perennial herb that grows 1-4 feet tall with smooth, arrow-shaped leaves that have a distinctive sour taste. This European native has spread throughout New England's grasslands and fields. The plant produces tall, slender spikes of small reddish-brown flowers in summer, and its leaves remain green and edible through much of the growing season.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Arrow-shaped leaves with backward-pointing lobes at the base, smooth edges, and a distinctly sour, lemony taste when chewed - like nature's candy with a pucker

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tall, narrow spikes of tiny reddish-brown flowers that start greenish and turn rusty red as they mature, creating an almost feathery appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps of upright stems 1-4 feet tall, often growing in patches from spreading underground roots

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are smooth to the touch with prominent veins, and the stem leaves clasp around the stem with their pointed basal lobes

habitat: Common sorrel thrives in meadows, fields, roadsides, and disturbed grasslands throughout New England. It prefers acidic soils and full sun to partial shade, often appearing in areas where the soil has been compacted or disturbed. You'll commonly find it growing alongside other weedy species in old fields and pastures.

seasonality.spring: Fresh arrow-shaped leaves emerge early and are at their most tender and flavorful for eating. This is when the sour taste is most pronounced and pleasant.
seasonality.summer: Tall flowering spikes appear, starting green and gradually turning reddish-brown. Leaves remain present but become somewhat tougher as the plant puts energy into reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and the flowering spikes turn a rusty brown color. Basal leaves may persist and can still be identified by their shape and sour taste.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, but the perennial roots remain alive underground, ready to send up new shoots in spring.

funFact: Common sorrel contains oxalic acid, the same compound that makes rhubarb sour, and has been used as a natural way to remove rust stains and polish copper cookware - it's literally a edible cleaning agent!
confusionNotes: Common sorrel is often confused with sheep's sorrel, but common sorrel is much larger with broader arrow-shaped leaves, while sheep's sorrel has smaller, narrower leaves that look more like tiny spearheads. Remember: 'common' means 'chunky' - it's the bigger, broader cousin.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse the edible common sorrel with wood sorrel (Oxalis), which has heart-shaped leaflets in groups of three and yellow flowers - they're completely unrelated plants that just happen to share a sour taste and similar name.
compareHints: Among the dock and sorrel family, common sorrel stands out with its distinctly arrow-shaped leaves and sour taste, while true docks like curled dock and broad-leaved dock have much larger, broader leaves without the pointed basal lobes and lack the sour flavor. Sheep's sorrel shares the sour taste but is much smaller with narrower, more spear-like leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its larger cousins the docks (broad-leaved dock, curled dock), sheep's sorrel stays much smaller and has those distinctive backward-pointing lobes on its leaves.

Among New England's dock species, broad-leaved dock is distinguished by its wide, flat-edged leaves – curled dock has wavy leaf margins, sheep's sorrel has arrow-shaped leaves, and swamp dock prefers wetland areas.
Among New England's dock species, curled dock is the easiest to identify thanks to its signature wavy leaf margins – no other dock has this feature.

Swamp dock differs from its dock relatives by its strong preference for wet habitats - while curled dock and broad-leaved dock are common weeds of dry disturbed soils, swamp dock sticks to marshes and wet areas.
Wood dock stands out dramatically from its dock relatives because of its red-veined leaves - no other dock species in New England has this feature.
Greater Water Dock stands apart from other New England docks by its wetland habitat and impressive size - it's notably larger than Curled Dock or Broad-leaved Dock.
Northern dock stands out from other Rumex species by its long, narrow leaves with smooth edges - most other docks have broader leaves or wavy margins like curled dock.
Unlike its inland relatives like curled dock or broad-leaved dock, seabeach dock has much thicker, fleshier leaves and stays much lower to the ground.

Pacific golden dock stands out from other New England dock species primarily by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most relatives like curled dock and broad-leaved dock have greenish or reddish blooms.
White willow dock stands out from its dock relatives by having much narrower leaves - compare this to broad-leaved dock or curled dock which have wide, often wavy-edged leaves.
Among its dock relatives in New England, willow dock stands out with its narrow leaves - most other docks like broad-leaved dock and curled dock have much wider foliage.

Golden dock differs from other New England docks by its much smaller stature and distinctive golden flower clusters - most other docks like curled dock or broad-leaved dock are much larger perennial plants with reddish-brown flower clusters.
Golden dock stands out from its dock relatives by having much narrower leaves - more like a willow than the typical broad, paddle-shaped dock leaf.
Patience dock stands out from other New England docks by its exceptionally large size and smooth-edged leaves with heart-shaped bases.
